content: The Center for Structural Genomics, the Center for Stem Cell Biology, and the Center for Structural Biology are key research programs. Additionally, the Michigan Bioinformatics Program is a significant initiative. The Medical Science I and II buildings, opened in 1958 and 1969 respectively, house the Medical School and University of Michigan Health System (UMHS) administrative offices, research laboratories, and faculty offices. Medical Science II serves as the primary facility for medical student education. The Medical Science Research Buildings I, II, and III were opened in 1986, 1989, and 1995, respectively. These buildings host basic research laboratories and shared core facilities for biomedical researchers at the University of Michigan. MSRB I also houses the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) offices, as the university was selected as one of 12 HHMI sites nationwide. The Kresge Complex, built between 1954 and 1963, includes the Kresge Medical Research buildings and the Kresge Hearing Research Institute. These facilities are home to research laboratories, including otolaryngology labs, the Michigan Diabetes Research & Training Center, the Upjohn Center for Clinical Pharmacology, and the Michigan Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, which recently received a $10 million grant. The Kresge buildings are identified in the UMHS Master Plan as sites for future development, likely to be replaced with new research facilities. The North Ingalls Building, an 11-story structure purchased by the university in 1977, was formerly the St. Joseph Mercy Hospital. It now houses administrative offices for U-M Hospitals & Health Centers and various clinical departments. The School of Public Health (SPH), established in 1941, is home to a top-rated clinical research program. In 2007, it was ranked 5 among Public Health Schools in the U.S. and has consistently ranked 1 in Health Management since 1993. In 2006, the SPH completed construction of the Crossroads and Research Tower, a seven-story, 125,000-square-foot building with 17 conference rooms and 133 laboratory benches. SPH is one of two lead institutions in the Finland-United States Investigation of Non-Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Genetics (FUSION) study group, which recently discovered four new genes associated with Type II Diabetes. It also houses the renowned U-M Autism and Communication Disorders Center, a leader in autism treatment and genetics research. SPH has 180 faculty members across five academic departments: Biostatistics, Environmental Health Science, Epidemiology, Health Behavior and Health Education, and Health Management and Policy. The East Ann Arbor Health and Geriatrics Center, opened in 1996 and renovated in 2006, provides outpatient clinics in general internal medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics & gynecology, and geriatric care. It includes a pharmacy, a patient education center, a blood-draw station, and imaging facilities for MRI, CT, and mammography. Specialty clinics tailored for elderly care include the Foot Care Clinic, Incontinence Clinic, Mobility Enhancement Clinic, Cognitive Disorders Clinic, Movement Disorders Clinic, Deep Brain Stimulation Clinic, Geropsychiatry Clinic, Sexual Health Clinic, Transitional Care Clinic, and Women’s Health Clinic. The Rachel Upjohn Depression Center, opened in 2006 near the Geriatrics Center, is the first Comprehensive Depression Center in the country. The 112,500-square-foot facility includes 335 offices and outpatient treatment rooms, a 120-seat auditorium, and telemedicine offices to assist patients in remote areas. It consolidates outpatient psychiatric and substance abuse care for adults and children into one facility and houses leading centers for the treatment of depression and bipolar disorder. The center also includes a library, an art gallery, and space for research, education, and administrative programs. It is named after Rachel Mary (Upjohn) Meader, who, along with her husband Edwin, donated $10 million toward its construction. The facility also features the Sleep Research Center, an MRI simulator, a Brain Imaging Center, and the Stress and Neuroendocrine Program. The MedSport Suite, located in a 45,000-square-foot facility at Domino’s Farms, houses the Sports Medicine Division of Orthopedic Surgery. It includes 15 examination rooms, on-site radiology, a Physical Therapy Treatment Center, an Athletic Performance Center, and an Aquatics Program. It is one of the premier sports medicine programs in the country, attracting patients nationwide. MedSport physicians serve as team physicians for the U-M Athletic Department and the USA Hockey National Team. The Spine Program, a comprehensive multidisciplinary facility, brings together orthopedic surgeons, neurosurgeons, physiatrists, physical therapists, and occupational therapists to provide integrated spine care.
